scenes.title: Airflow XComs & TaskGroups
scenes.narration: This lesson covers two features that make complex Airflow DAGs manageable: XComs for passing data between tasks and TaskGroups for organizing them.

scenes.title: What XComs are
bullets: A pushed return value can be pulled downstream
scenes.narration: XCom stands for cross-communication and is Airflow's mechanism for passing small pieces of data between tasks. A task can push a value, typically just by returning it, and a downstream task can pull that value to use in its own logic. These values are stored in Airflow's metadata database, which is exactly why they are meant to stay small.

scenes.title: Passing data with XComs
scenes.narration: Using the modern TaskFlow API, XComs feel almost invisible. The get_row_count task returns a value, which Airflow automatically pushes to XCom. When we pass its result into the report task, Airflow wires up the dependency and pulls the value for us. Under the hood this is still an XCom push and pull, but the decorator syntax lets you write it like ordinary Python function calls.

scenes.text: XComs are for small metadata like counts, filenames, or dates, never large datasets; pass big data by writing to storage and sharing the path.
scenes.narration: A critical warning: because XComs live in the metadata database, use them only for small metadata like row counts, filenames, or dates. For large datasets, write the data to object storage and pass only the path through XCom, keeping your database healthy.

scenes.title: What TaskGroups do
bullets: Visually and logically group related tasks
Collapse into a single node in the UI
scenes.narration: TaskGroups let you bundle related tasks together, both logically in your code and visually in the graph view where the group collapses into a single node. This keeps a DAG with dozens of tasks readable. Importantly, a TaskGroup is a purely organizational construct with no runtime overhead, unlike the older SubDAG feature it replaced.

scenes.title: Organizing with a TaskGroup
scenes.code:
from airflow.utils.task_group import TaskGroup

with TaskGroup(group_id='transform') as transform:
    stg = BashOperator(task_id='staging', bash_command='dbt run -s staging')
    marts = BashOperator(task_id='marts', bash_command='dbt run -s marts')
    stg >> marts

extract >> transform >> load
scenes.narration: Here we wrap two dbt steps in a TaskGroup named transform. Inside the group we still declare ordering between staging and marts. The powerful part is the last line: we can set dependencies on the entire group as a unit, so extract flows into the whole transform group and then into load. This lets you reason about the DAG at a high level while preserving the detail inside each group.

scenes.text: Use XComs for lightweight coordination and TaskGroups for structure, and your large DAGs stay both correct and readable.
scenes.narration: The lesson to remember is to use XComs for lightweight coordination between tasks and TaskGroups to give large DAGs structure, and together they keep even sprawling pipelines both correct and readable.
